transcript.text: I confirmed with our EPL insurer's claims administrator today that the policy requires written insurer notice and written consent before the company admits liability or provides any monetary resolution connected to this investigation. transcript.text: Thank you, Theo. From the HR perspective, this substantiated retaliation finding has significant implications for the corrective-action package. Given the minimum corrective action of a final written warning, combined with the complainant's transfer to the Product Compliance team and the 90-day no-contact request, I want to flag for the group that we now have several interlocking requirements to satisfy before closure. First, Elias has confirmed that Audit Committee notice is a hard prerequisite before we can close, given the director-level substantiated retaliation finding. Second, Ruth has confirmed that if the corrective-action package involves any admission of liability or monetary resolution, we need written insurer consent. And third, from HR's side, the complainant's agreed transfer and 90-day no-supervisory-contact request need to be formalized as part of any corrective-action package. I would recommend we do not attempt to close today until we've addressed the Audit Committee notice requirement and confirmed with Ruth whether the corrective-action elements trigger the insurer-notice obligation. transcript.text: Thank you, Nadia and Elias. From the insurance side, I want to directly answer the question about whether the corrective-action elements trigger the insurer-notice obligation. Based on what I confirmed with the EPL insurer's claims administrator today, the policy requirement is specific: we need written insurer notice and written consent before the company admits liability or provides any monetary resolution connected to this investigation. So the key triggers are an admission of liability or any monetary resolution — including settlement payments, severance, or similar monetary accommodations tied to this matter. A final written warning alone may not trigger that obligation, but if the complainant's transfer, the 90-day no-contact arrangement, or any other element of the corrective-action package is structured as a monetary accommodation or framed as an admission of liability, then the insurer-notice and consent requirement would apply. I would recommend that we carefully review the proposed corrective-action package language with that in mind before anything is finalized. I agree with the recommendation to hold closure in abeyance until both the Audit Committee notice and the insurer-notice analysis are completed.
